claim: PACT protein levels were significantly reduced in shPACT MEFs compared to control MEFs infected with control lentiviral vector.
source: We suppressed PACT expression in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) by lentiviral delivery of an shRNA directed against PACT. In these stable knockdown shPACT MEFs, PACT protein levels were significantly reduced compared to MEFs infected with the control lentiviral vector (shCon) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1B shows reduced PACT protein levels in shPACT cells, and the text explicitly states this reduction.

claim: Decrease in Prkra led to a substantial reduction in PKR activation at high-intensity hyperosmotic stress (600 mOsm) as measured by PKR phosphorylation at Serine-451.
source: Decrease in Prkra led to a substantial reduction in PKR activation at high-intensity hyperosmotic stress (600 mOsm) as measured by PKR phosphorylation at Serine-451 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1B shows reduced PKR-P451 levels in shPACT cells treated with 600 mOsm.

claim: Reduction in PKR activation correlated with the reduction of phosphorylation of PKR substrate eIF2α at serine-51.
source: This reduction in PKR activation correlated with the reduction of phosphorylation of PKR substrate eIF2α at serine-51.
evidence: The text states a correlation between reduced PKR activation and reduced eIF2α phosphorylation, supported by western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: PACT is necessary for PKR activation and downstream signaling in high intensity hyperosmotic stress conditions.
source: This suggests that PACT is necessary for PKR activation and downstream signaling in high intensity hyperosmotic stress conditions.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that PACT knockdown reduces PKR activation and eIF2α phosphorylation.

claim: PKR and PACT interact at three distinct protein domains with varying degrees of specificity.
source: It has previously been shown that PKR and PACT interact at three distinct protein domains with varying degrees of specificity (Peters et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peters et al., 2001.

claim: In unstressed or low-intensity stress conditions (500 mOsm sucrose or 5% w/v DSS), there was no PACT-PKR interaction.
source: In unstressed or low-intensity stress conditions (500 mOsm sucrose or 5% w/v DSS), we found no PACT-PKR interaction; however, in high-intensity stress conditions (600 mOsm sucrose or 10% w/v DSS), PACT-PKR existed in a complex, suggesting stress intensity-induced binding (Figure 1C).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1C shows no PACT band in low-intensity conditions.

claim: In high-intensity stress conditions (600 mOsm sucrose or 10% w/v DSS), PACT-PKR existed in a complex, suggesting stress intensity-induced binding.
source: In unstressed or low-intensity stress conditions (500 mOsm sucrose or 5% w/v DSS), we found no PACT-PKR interaction; however, in high-intensity stress conditions (600 mOsm sucrose or 10% w/v DSS), PACT-PKR existed in a complex, suggesting stress intensity-induced binding (Figure 1C).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1C shows PACT band in high-intensity conditions.

claim: Phosphorylation of PACT at Ser-287 occurs in response to various cellular stresses and depends upon prior phosphorylation of Ser-246.
source: Phosphorylation of Ser-287 occurs in response to various cellular stresses, and depends upon prior phosphorylation of Ser-246 (Peters et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peters et al., 2006.

claim: When PACT KO MEFs were reconstituted with PACT bearing a mutated phosphosite at residue 287 (S287A) or at residue 246 (S246A), interaction with PKR was diminished compared to wild type PACT control.
source: When PACT KO MEFs were reconstituted with PACT bearing a mutated phosphosite at residue 287 (S287A), or at its prerequisite phosphosite residue 246 (S246A), interaction with PKR was diminished compared to the wild type (WT) PACT control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows reduced PKR binding to S246A and S287A PACT mutants.

claim: Lacking phosphorylation sites at Ser-246 and Ser-287, PKR was unable to be activated as measured by its autophosphorylation at Thr-451.
source: Lacking these phosphorylation sites, and the interaction with PKR that depends on the modification of these residues, PKR was unable to be activated as measured by its autophosphorylation at Thr-451 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows reduced PKR-P451 in S246A and S287A PACT mutants.

claim: In response to high-intensity hyperosmotic stress, PACT phosphorylation at residues Ser-246 and Ser-287 promote its interaction with PKR to activate its kinase activity.
source: Together, these data indicate that in response to high-intensity hyperosmotic stress, PACT phosphorylation at residues Ser-246 and Ser-287 promote its interaction with PKR to activate its kinase activity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mutational analysis showing that S246A and S287A mutations reduce PKR interaction and activation.

claim: shPACT cells showed significantly reduced caspase-3 activity compared to control cells at high-intensity hyperosmotic stress.
source: We found that shPACT cells showed significantly reduced caspase-3 activity, suggesting that PACT has a pro-apoptotic role in high-intensity hyperosmotic stress conditions (Figure 1D), similar to PKR (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: Caspase-3 activity assay data in Figure 1D shows reduced activity in shPACT cells at 600 mOsm.

claim: PACT has a pro-apoptotic role in high-intensity hyperosmotic stress conditions.
source: We found that shPACT cells showed significantly reduced caspase-3 activity, suggesting that PACT has a pro-apoptotic role in high-intensity hyperosmotic stress conditions (Figure 1D), similar to PKR (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: The inference is based on reduced caspase-3 activity in PACT-deficient cells.

claim: At low intensity stress conditions, there is neither any increase in caspase-3 activity nor interaction between PACT and PKR.
source: Combined with Figure 1C, these data demonstrate that at low intensity stress conditions, there is neither any increase in caspase-3 activity nor interaction between PACT and PKR; PACT-PKR interaction and increased apoptosis only occur in high-intensity hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C (no PACT-PKR interaction at low intensity) and Figure 1D (no caspase-3 increase at low intensity).

claim: PACT-PKR interaction and increased apoptosis only occur in high-intensity hyperosmotic stress.
source: Combined with Figure 1C, these data demonstrate that at low intensity stress conditions, there is neither any increase in caspase-3 activity nor interaction between PACT and PKR; PACT-PKR interaction and increased apoptosis only occur in high-intensity hyperosmotic stress.
evidence: This is supported by data showing PACT-PKR interaction and increased caspase-3 activity only at high intensity.

claim: Expression of proinflammatory genes such as iNOS and IL6 are induced in high-intensity hyperosmotic conditions and are in part dependent on signaling downstream of PKR activation.
source: We have previously shown that expression of proinflammatory genes such as iNOS and IL6 are induced in high-intensity hyperosmotic conditions, and are in part dependent on signaling downstream of PKR activation (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: Loss of PACT led to a decrease in mRNA induction of proinflammatory genes Nos2 and Il6 under high intensity stress.
source: We found that loss of PACT led to a decrease in mRNA induction of several proinflammatory genes such as Nos2 and Il6 under high intensity stress (Figure 1E).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 1E shows reduced Nos2 and Il6 mRNA levels in shPACT cells at 600 mOsm.

claim: Nos2 mRNA induction was decreased in MEFs in which PACT phosphorylation at Ser-246 and Ser-287 was impaired.
source: Further supporting the role of PACT-PKR signaling in high stress-induced inflammatory gene expression, we found that Nos2 mRNA induction was also decreased in MEFs in which PACT phosphorylation at Ser-246 and Ser-287 was impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and in which the kinase function of PKR was inactive by mutation of the catalytic lysine residue in the active site to arginine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C shows reduced Nos2 mRNA in S246A PACT mutant.

claim: Nos2 mRNA induction was decreased in MEFs in which the kinase function of PKR was inactive by mutation of the catalytic lysine residue in the active site to arginine.
source: Further supporting the role of PACT-PKR signaling in high stress-induced inflammatory gene expression, we found that Nos2 mRNA induction was also decreased in MEFs in which PACT phosphorylation at Ser-246 and Ser-287 was impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and in which the kinase function of PKR was inactive by mutation of the catalytic lysine residue in the active site to arginine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D shows reduced Nos2 mRNA in K296R PKR mutant.

claim: The ability of PKR to bind to dsRNA did not affect Nos2 mRNA levels in hyperosmotic stress conditions.
source: The ability of PKR to bind to dsRNA did not affect Nos2 mRNA levels in hyperosmotic stress conditions, as demonstrated by impairment of RNA binding via double mutation of key residues involved in this interaction, Lys-64 and Lys-154 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D shows similar Nos2 mRNA levels in K64R/K154R PKR mutant compared to wild type.

claim: Functional PACT-PKR signaling is necessary for maximal expression of a subset of inflammatory genes.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that functional PACT-PKR signaling is necessary for maximal expression of a subset of inflammatory genes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that disrupting PACT-PKR signaling reduces inflammatory gene expression.

claim: Induction of osmoadaptive Slc38a2 mRNA levels was unaffected after 3 hr of low-intensity stress treatment in cells depleted of PACT.
source: Finally, induction of osmoadaptive Slc38a2 mRNA levels was unaffected after 3 hr of low-intensity stress treatment in cells depleted of PACT (Figure 1E); the decrease after 5 hr of low-intensity treatment may be a result of downstream PACT signaling on post-transcriptional mechanisms on Slc38a2 mRNA accumulation.
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 1E shows similar Slc38a2 mRNA levels in shPACT and control cells at 3 hr 500 mOsm.

claim: The decrease in Slc38a2 mRNA after 5 hr of low-intensity treatment in PACT-depleted cells may be a result of downstream PACT signaling on post-transcriptional mechanisms on Slc38a2 mRNA accumulation.
source: Finally, induction of osmoadaptive Slc38a2 mRNA levels was unaffected after 3 hr of low-intensity stress treatment in cells depleted of PACT (Figure 1E); the decrease after 5 hr of low-intensity treatment may be a result of downstream PACT signaling on post-transcriptional mechanisms on Slc38a2 mRNA accumulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed decrease at 5 hr.

claim: The decrease in osmoadaptive mRNA levels in PACT-depleted cells did not lead to caspase-3 activity or apoptosis under low intensity hyperosmotic stress.
source: This decrease in osmoadaptive mRNA levels did not lead to caspase-3 activity or apoptosis under low intensity hyperosmotic stress (Figure 1D).
evidence: Caspase-3 activity data in Figure 1D shows no significant increase in shPACT cells at 500 mOsm.

claim: TonEBP translocates to the nucleus in response to an increase in osmolarity to regulate transcription of target genes associated with osmoadaptation.
source: TonEBP translocates to the nucleus in response to an increase in osmolarity to regulate transcription of target genes associated with osmoadaptation (Miyakawa et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miyakawa et al., 1999.

claim: TonEBP target genes include chaperone proteins (heat shock protein 70 [HSP70, Hspa1a]).
source: These include chaperone proteins (heat shock protein 70 [HSP70, Hspa1a]; Woo et al., 2002), enzymes involved in biosynthesis of neutral osmolytes (aldose reductase [AR, Akr1b1]; Ferraris et al., 1994), and membrane proteins that transport organic osmolytes such as amino acids proline and alanine across the plasma membrane (sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter [SNAT2, Slc38a2]; Trama et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Woo et al., 2002.

claim: TonEBP target genes include enzymes involved in biosynthesis of neutral osmolytes (aldose reductase [AR, Akr1b1]).
source: These include chaperone proteins (heat shock protein 70 [HSP70, Hspa1a]; Woo et al., 2002), enzymes involved in biosynthesis of neutral osmolytes (aldose reductase [AR, Akr1b1]; Ferraris et al., 1994), and membrane proteins that transport organic osmolytes such as amino acids proline and alanine across the plasma membrane (sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter [SNAT2, Slc38a2]; Trama et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ferraris et al., 1994.

claim: TonEBP target genes include membrane proteins that transport organic osmolytes such as amino acids proline and alanine across the plasma membrane (sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter [SNAT2, Slc38a2]).
source: These include chaperone proteins (heat shock protein 70 [HSP70, Hspa1a]; Woo et al., 2002), enzymes involved in biosynthesis of neutral osmolytes (aldose reductase [AR, Akr1b1]; Ferraris et al., 1994), and membrane proteins that transport organic osmolytes such as amino acids proline and alanine across the plasma membrane (sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter [SNAT2, Slc38a2]; Trama et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Trama et al., 2002.

claim: The SNAT2-mediated arm of the adaptive response is also dependent on the membrane trafficking function of PP1/GADD34.
source: The SNAT2-mediated arm of the adaptive response is also dependent on the membrane trafficking function of PP1/GADD34 (Krokowski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krokowski et al., 2017.

claim: Extracellular osmolarities of 500 and 600 mOsm are representative of low stress intensity/adaptive response and high stress intensity/non-adaptive response, respectively, in MEFs.
source: We have previously determined in MEFs that extracellular osmolarities of 500 and 600 mOsm are representative of low stress intensity/adaptive response and high stress intensity/non-adaptive response, respectively (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with an increase in NF-κB activation.
source: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with an increase in NF-κB activation (Németh et al., 2002) and inflammation (Müller et al., 2019), as well as production and release of multiple proinflammatory cytokines, including IL8 (10), TNFα (Lang et al., 2002), IL1β (Ip and Medzhitov, 2015), and IL6 (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Németh et al., 2002.

claim: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with inflammation.
source: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with an increase in NF-κB activation (Németh et al., 2002) and inflammation (Müller et al., 2019), as well as production and release of multiple proinflammatory cytokines, including IL8 (10), TNFα (Lang et al., 2002), IL1β (Ip and Medzhitov, 2015), and IL6 (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Müller et al., 2019.

claim: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with production and release of TNFα.
source: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with an increase in NF-κB activation (Németh et al., 2002) and inflammation (Müller et al., 2019), as well as production and release of multiple proinflammatory cytokines, including IL8 (10), TNFα (Lang et al., 2002), IL1β (Ip and Medzhitov, 2015), and IL6 (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lang et al., 2002.

claim: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with production and release of IL1β.
source: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with an increase in NF-κB activation (Németh et al., 2002) and inflammation (Müller et al., 2019), as well as production and release of multiple proinflammatory cytokines, including IL8 (10), TNFα (Lang et al., 2002), IL1β (Ip and Medzhitov, 2015), and IL6 (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ip and Medzhitov, 2015.

claim: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with production and release of IL6.
source: An increase in hyperosmolarity is associated with an increase in NF-κB activation (Németh et al., 2002) and inflammation (Müller et al., 2019), as well as production and release of multiple proinflammatory cytokines, including IL8 (10), TNFα (Lang et al., 2002), IL1β (Ip and Medzhitov, 2015), and IL6 (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Igarashi et al., 2014.

claim: Apoptosis following hyperosmotic stress is characterized by depolarization of mitochondria leading to an increase in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio.
source: Apoptosis following hyperosmotic stress is characterized by depolarization of mitochondria leading to an increase in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio (Michea et al., 2002), as well as sometimes by clustering and internalization of TNFα receptors (Rosette and Karin, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Michea et al., 2002.

claim: Apoptosis following hyperosmotic stress is sometimes characterized by clustering and internalization of TNFα receptors.
source: Apoptosis following hyperosmotic stress is characterized by depolarization of mitochondria leading to an increase in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio (Michea et al., 2002), as well as sometimes by clustering and internalization of TNFα receptors (Rosette and Karin, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rosette and Karin, 1996.

claim: NF-κB-dependent signaling is pro-apoptotic in high-intensity hyperosmotic stress, in part via induction of inducible nitric oxide synthetase (iNOS).
source: We have previously shown that NF-κB-dependent signaling is pro-apoptotic in high-intensity hyperosmotic stress, in part via induction of inducible nitric oxide synthetase (iNOS) (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: NF-κB p65 is phosphorylated and accumulates in the nucleus in hyperosmotic conditions.
source: NF-κB p65 is phosphorylated and accumulates in the nucleus in hyperosmotic conditions, and induces the transcription of a number of proinflammatory target genes, such as Nos2 (Jia et al., 2013), Il6 (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and Tnfa (Iwata et al., 1999), as well as caspase 3/9 activation (Eisner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: NF-κB p65 induces the transcription of proinflammatory target gene Nos2.
source: NF-κB p65 is phosphorylated and accumulates in the nucleus in hyperosmotic conditions, and induces the transcription of a number of proinflammatory target genes, such as Nos2 (Jia et al., 2013), Il6 (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and Tnfa (Iwata et al., 1999), as well as caspase 3/9 activation (Eisner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jia et al., 2013.

claim: NF-κB p65 induces the transcription of proinflammatory target gene Il6.
source: NF-κB p65 is phosphorylated and accumulates in the nucleus in hyperosmotic conditions, and induces the transcription of a number of proinflammatory target genes, such as Nos2 (Jia et al., 2013), Il6 (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and Tnfa (Iwata et al., 1999), as well as caspase 3/9 activation (Eisner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Farabaugh et al., 2017.

claim: NF-κB p65 induces the transcription of proinflammatory target gene Tnfa.
source: NF-κB p65 is phosphorylated and accumulates in the nucleus in hyperosmotic conditions, and induces the transcription of a number of proinflammatory target genes, such as Nos2 (Jia et al., 2013), Il6 (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and Tnfa (Iwata et al., 1999), as well as caspase 3/9 activation (Eisner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Iwata et al., 1999.

claim: NF-κB p65 induces caspase 3/9 activation.
source: NF-κB p65 is phosphorylated and accumulates in the nucleus in hyperosmotic conditions, and induces the transcription of a number of proinflammatory target genes, such as Nos2 (Jia et al., 2013), Il6 (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and Tnfa (Iwata et al., 1999), as well as caspase 3/9 activation (Eisner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eisner et al., 2006.

claim: NF-κB p65 is necessary for initiation of the inflammatory response in response to LPS.
source: NF-κB p65 is necessary for initiation of the inflammatory response in response to LPS (McDonald et al., 1997; Hobbs et al., 2018), for the development of Th17 cells via induction of the transcription factor RORγ (Ruan et al., 2011a), and for pathology in many diseases with inflammatory components, including inflammatory bowel disease (Han et al., 2018; Schreiber et al., 1998) and dry eye syndrome (Tan et al., 2018; He et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McDonald et al., 1997 and Hobbs et al., 2018.

claim: NF-κB p65 is necessary for the development of Th17 cells via induction of the transcription factor RORγ.
source: NF-κB p65 is necessary for initiation of the inflammatory response in response to LPS (McDonald et al., 1997; Hobbs et al., 2018), for the development of Th17 cells via induction of the transcription factor RORγ (Ruan et al., 2011a), and for pathology in many diseases with inflammatory components, including inflammatory bowel disease (Han et al., 2018; Schreiber et al., 1998) and dry eye syndrome (Tan et al., 2018; He et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ruan et al., 2011a.

claim: NF-κB p65 is necessary for pathology in inflammatory bowel disease.
source: NF-κB p65 is necessary for initiation of the inflammatory response in response to LPS (McDonald et al., 1997; Hobbs et al., 2018), for the development of Th17 cells via induction of the transcription factor RORγ (Ruan et al., 2011a), and for pathology in many diseases with inflammatory components, including inflammatory bowel disease (Han et al., 2018; Schreiber et al., 1998) and dry eye syndrome (Tan et al., 2018; He et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Han et al., 2018 and Schreiber et al., 1998.

claim: NF-κB p65 is necessary for pathology in dry eye syndrome.
source: NF-κB p65 is necessary for initiation of the inflammatory response in response to LPS (McDonald et al., 1997; Hobbs et al., 2018), for the development of Th17 cells via induction of the transcription factor RORγ (Ruan et al., 2011a), and for pathology in many diseases with inflammatory components, including inflammatory bowel disease (Han et al., 2018; Schreiber et al., 1998) and dry eye syndrome (Tan et al., 2018; He et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tan et al., 2018 and He et al., 2011.

claim: Simultaneous deletion of Tnfa in NF-κB p65 knockout mice leads to survival, demonstrating that NF-κB p65 plays a role in the prevention of TNF-induced toxicity during development.
source: Although deletion of NF-κB p65 is embryonically lethal in mice, simultaneous deletion of Tnfa leads to survival, and demonstrates that NF-κB p65 plays a role in the prevention of TNF-induced toxicity during development (Doi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doi et al., 1999.

claim: c-Rel is required for transcription of Irf4, which promotes proliferation of B cells.
source: c-Rel is required for transcription of many genes necessary for immune system function, including Irf4, which promotes proliferation of B cells (Grumont and Gerondakis, 2000), Bcl2l1 and Bcl2A1, which promote survival of B cells (Owyang et al., 2001), and Il21, which promotes development of Th17 cells (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grumont and Gerondakis, 2000.

claim: c-Rel is required for transcription of Bcl2l1 and Bcl2A1, which promote survival of B cells.
source: c-Rel is required for transcription of many genes necessary for immune system function, including Irf4, which promotes proliferation of B cells (Grumont and Gerondakis, 2000), Bcl2l1 and Bcl2A1, which promote survival of B cells (Owyang et al., 2001), and Il21, which promotes development of Th17 cells (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Owyang et al., 2001.

claim: c-Rel is required for transcription of Il21, which promotes development of Th17 cells.
source: c-Rel is required for transcription of many genes necessary for immune system function, including Irf4, which promotes proliferation of B cells (Grumont and Gerondakis, 2000), Bcl2l1 and Bcl2A1, which promote survival of B cells (Owyang et al., 2001), and Il21, which promotes development of Th17 cells (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: c-Rel KO mice are resistant to EAE, an autoimmune model of multiple sclerosis driven by Th17 cells.
source: c-Rel-deficiency leads to altered phenotypes in many disease models: c-Rel KO mice are resistant to EAE, an autoimmune model of multiple sclerosis driven by Th17 cells (Chen et al., 2011); c-Rel KO mice fail to develop severe colitis induced by treatment with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)(Luu et al., 2017), perhaps also as a result of loss of Th17 cell development (Chen et al., 2011); and overexpression of c-Rel has been shown to protect human islets from cell death mediated by the cell death protein PDCD4 via an increase in microRNA-21 expression (Ruan et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: c-Rel KO mice fail to develop severe colitis induced by treatment with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS).
source: c-Rel-deficiency leads to altered phenotypes in many disease models: c-Rel KO mice are resistant to EAE, an autoimmune model of multiple sclerosis driven by Th17 cells (Chen et al., 2011); c-Rel KO mice fail to develop severe colitis induced by treatment with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)(Luu et al., 2017), perhaps also as a result of loss of Th17 cell development (Chen et al., 2011); and overexpression of c-Rel has been shown to protect human islets from cell death mediated by the cell death protein PDCD4 via an increase in microRNA-21 expression (Ruan et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Luu et al., 2017.

claim: Overexpression of c-Rel has been shown to protect human islets from cell death mediated by the cell death protein PDCD4 via an increase in microRNA-21 expression.
source: c-Rel-deficiency leads to altered phenotypes in many disease models: c-Rel KO mice are resistant to EAE, an autoimmune model of multiple sclerosis driven by Th17 cells (Chen et al., 2011); c-Rel KO mice fail to develop severe colitis induced by treatment with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)(Luu et al., 2017), perhaps also as a result of loss of Th17 cell development (Chen et al., 2011); and overexpression of c-Rel has been shown to protect human islets from cell death mediated by the cell death protein PDCD4 via an increase in microRNA-21 expression (Ruan et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ruan et al., 2011b.

claim: PKR promotes the nuclear localization of Serine-536 phosphorylated NF-κB family member p65, which leads to an increase in inflammatory gene induction and cell death.
source: We have shown that protein kinase R (PKR) promotes the nuclear localization of Serine-536 phosphorylated NF-κB family member p65, which leads to an increase in inflammatory gene induction and cell death (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: PKR is activated under hyperosmotic stress.
source: PKR is activated under hyperosmotic stress (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and it has also been shown previously to regulate NF-κB signaling in inflammatory conditions, via the direct phosphorylation of the inhibitor of κB (IκB; Kumar et al., 1994) or interaction with the inhibitor of κB kinase (IKK; Ishii et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Farabaugh et al., 2017.

claim: PKR regulates NF-κB signaling in inflammatory conditions via the direct phosphorylation of the inhibitor of κB (IκB).
source: PKR is activated under hyperosmotic stress (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and it has also been shown previously to regulate NF-κB signaling in inflammatory conditions, via the direct phosphorylation of the inhibitor of κB (IκB; Kumar et al., 1994) or interaction with the inhibitor of κB kinase (IKK; Ishii et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kumar et al., 1994.

claim: PKR regulates NF-κB signaling in inflammatory conditions via interaction with the inhibitor of κB kinase (IKK).
source: PKR is activated under hyperosmotic stress (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and it has also been shown previously to regulate NF-κB signaling in inflammatory conditions, via the direct phosphorylation of the inhibitor of κB (IκB; Kumar et al., 1994) or interaction with the inhibitor of κB kinase (IKK; Ishii et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2001.

claim: PKR activation and downstream NF-κB signaling were evident after high intensity hyperosmotic treatment with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS, 10%) in cell culture.
source: PKR activation and downstream NF-κB signaling were also evident after high intensity hyperosmotic treatment with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS, 10%) in cell culture (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: Adaptation to low intensity hyperosmotic treatment (5% DSS) was observed.
source: In contrast, we observed adaptation to low intensity hyperosmotic treatment (5% DSS)(Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: PKR phosphorylates Ser-51 of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 α subunit (eIF2α), contributing to inhibition of global mRNA translation.
source: PKR phosphorylates Ser-51 of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 α subunit (eIF2α), contributing to inhibition of global mRNA translation (Saelens et al., 2001; Bevilacqua et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Saelens et al., 2001 and Bevilacqua et al., 2010.

claim: The binding of dsRNA is unnecessary for PKR activation and downstream eIF2α phosphorylation in hyperosmotic conditions.
source: Although PKR is classically activated by the binding of viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) to the dsRNA-binding domain, we have shown that the binding of dsRNA is unnecessary for PKR activation and downstream eIF2α phosphorylation in hyperosmotic conditions (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: PACT can bind PKR at several domains including the two dsRNA-binding domains and the N-terminal portion of the kinase domain.
source: PACT is a dsRNA-binding protein that can bind PKR at several domains including the two dsRNA-binding domains and the N-terminal portion of the kinase domain (Peters et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peters et al., 2001.

claim: PACT interaction with the kinase domain of PKR inhibits its closed conformation and promotes an open, active conformation.
source: PACT interaction with the kinase domain of PKR, inhibits its closed conformation and promotes an open, active conformation (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2006.

claim: Similar patterns in TonEBP nuclear localization were found upon PACT depletion either at low or at high stress intensity.
source: We found similar patterns in TonEBP nuclear localization upon PACT depletion either at low or at high stress intensity (Figure 2A).
evidence: Western blot data of nuclear fractions in Figure 2A shows similar TonEBP levels in shPACT cells at both stress intensities.

claim: TonEBP alone may not be sufficient to induce maximum levels of expression of osmoadaptive genes in response to hyperosmotic conditions irrespective of stress intensity.
source: This indicates that TonEBP alone may not be sufficient to induce maximum levels of expression of osmoadaptive genes in response to hyperosmotic conditions irrespective of stress intensity.
evidence: This inference is drawn from the observation that TonEBP nuclear localization is similar at both stress intensities despite different gene expression outcomes.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of NF-κB c-Rel was found at lower intensity in the absence of PACT.
source: Interestingly, we found nuclear accumulation of the NF-κB family member c-Rel at lower intensity in the absence of PACT (Figure 2A).
evidence: Western blot data of nuclear fractions in Figure 2A shows increased c-Rel in shPACT cells at 500 mOsm.

claim: Depletion of PACT decreases total NF-κB p65 and NF-κB p65-P(Ser-536) accumulation in the nucleus.
source: In contrast to increased c-Rel, depletion of PACT decreases total NF-κB p65 and NF-κB p65-P(Ser-536) accumulation in the nucleus (Figure 2A), which may result in a decrease in NF-κB p65-mediated activation of proinflammatory genes.
evidence: Western blot data of nuclear fractions in Figure 2A shows decreased p65 and p65-P536 in shPACT cells.

claim: A deficiency in PACT did not affect cell survival at low intensity hyperosmotic conditions.
source: Although PACT-mediated PKR activation appears to decrease cell survival during high intensity hyperosmotic stress, a deficiency in PACT did not affect cell survival at low intensity hyperosmotic conditions, and correlated with an increase in nuclear localization of NF-κB c-Rel (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of caspase-3 activity increase in shPACT cells at 500 mOsm (Figure 1D).

claim: shc-Rel MEFs had higher levels of caspase-3 activity when treated with 500 mOsm medium.
source: When treated with 500 mOsm medium, shc-Rel MEFs had higher levels of caspase-3 activity (Figure 2B), suggesting a pro-survival role for NF-κB c-Rel.
evidence: Caspase-3 activity assay data in Figure 2B shows increased activity in shc-Rel cells at 500 mOsm.

claim: NF-κB c-Rel has a pro-survival role in low-intensity hyperosmotic stress.
source: When treated with 500 mOsm medium, shc-Rel MEFs had higher levels of caspase-3 activity (Figure 2B), suggesting a pro-survival role for NF-κB c-Rel.
evidence: This inference is drawn from increased caspase-3 activity in c-Rel-deficient cells.

claim: When cells are depleted of NF-κB c-Rel, NF-κB p65-P(Ser-536) accumulates in the nucleus at low intensity hyperosmotic stress.
source: Indeed, when cells are depleted of NF-κB c-Rel, NF-κB p65-P(Ser-536) accumulates in the nucleus at low intensity hyperosmotic stress (Figure 2C), a hallmark of the apoptotic signaling pathway previously identified (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: Western blot data of nuclear fractions in Figure 2C shows increased p65-P536 in shc-Rel cells at 500 mOsm.

claim: The increase in NF-κB p65-P(Ser-536) in c-Rel-depleted cells correlates with an increase in iNOS mRNA levels.
source: This increase in NF-κB p65-P(Ser-536) correlates with an increase in iNOS mRNA levels (Figure 2D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 2D shows increased Nos2 mRNA in shc-Rel cells.

claim: NF-κB c-Rel is a novel factor in the transition from adaptation to proinflammatory gene expression programs with increasing stress intensity.
source: These data suggest that NF-κB c-Rel is a novel factor in the transition from adaptation to proinflammatory gene expression programs with increasing stress intensity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that c-Rel depletion leads to increased inflammatory signaling at low stress intensity.

claim: The low stress-mediated induction of osmoadaptive gene targets SNAT2 and GADD34 are dependent on TonEBP.
source: First we confirmed that the low stress-mediated induction of osmoadaptive gene targets SNAT2 and GADD34 are dependent on TonEBP in our experimental system (Figure 2E).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 2E shows reduced Slc38a2 and Ppp1r15a mRNA in TonEBP KO cells at 500 mOsm.

claim: Transcription of Slc38a2 and Ppp1r15a is diminished in NF-κB c-Rel-suppressed cells.
source: We found that transcription of Slc38a2 and Ppp1r15a is indeed diminished in NF-κB c-Rel-suppressed cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 2F shows reduced Slc38a2 and Ppp1r15a mRNA in shc-Rel cells.

claim: SNAT2 and GADD34 are gene targets of the NF-κB c-Rel-mediated adaptive response.
source: These data identify SNAT2 and GADD34 as gene targets not only of the TonEBP-mediated transcriptional response to hyperosmotic stress, but also of the NF-κB c-Rel-mediated adaptive response.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that both TonEBP and c-Rel are required for full induction of these genes.

claim: The dependence of osmoadaptation on NF-κB c-Rel is a new finding in the literature.
source: To our knowledge, the dependence of osmoadaptation on NF-κB c-Rel is a new finding in the literature.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: The reduction in Slc38a2 mRNA in shc-Rel MEFs led to reduced protein levels in both immature, unprocessed SNAT2 and the mature glycosylated form.
source: The reduction in Slc38a2 mRNA in shc-Rel MEFs led to reduced protein levels in both immature, unprocessed SNAT2 and the mature glycosylated form, as determined by western blot analysis of cytoplasmic membrane fractions (Figure 2G).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2G shows reduced SNAT2 protein in shc-Rel cells.

claim: GADD34 protein levels were reduced in shc-Rel MEFs.
source: GADD34 protein levels were also reduced in shc-Rel MEFs (Figure 2H).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2H shows reduced GADD34 protein in shc-Rel cells.

claim: Decreased protein levels of both SNAT2 and GADD34 resulted in decreased SNAT2 functionality, as measured via uptake of the amino acid proline.
source: As expected, decreased protein levels of both SNAT2 and GADD34 resulted in decreased SNAT2 functionality, as measured via uptake of the amino acid proline (Figure 2I).
evidence: Proline uptake assay data in Figure 2I shows reduced uptake in shc-Rel cells.

claim: The luciferase activity under control of both Slc38a2 and Ppp1r15a promoters were much less responsive under hyperosmotic conditions in shc-Rel MEFs and TonEBP-/- MEFs compared to controls.
source: We found that the luciferase activity under control of both Slc38a2 and Ppp1r15a promoters were much less responsive under hyperosmotic conditions in shc-Rel MEFs and TonEBP-/- MEFs compared to controls (Figure 2J–K).
evidence: Luciferase assay data in Figure 2J-K shows reduced activity in shc-Rel and TonEBP KO cells.

claim: NF-κB c-Rel contributes to adaptation to hyperosmotic conditions at least in part via the SNAT2-dependent arm of the adaptive program.
source: These results suggest that NF-κB c-Rel contributes to adaptation to hyperosmotic conditions at least in part via the SNAT2-dependent arm of the adaptive program.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that c-Rel is required for SNAT2 expression and function.

claim: DSS treatment of cells in culture results in similar patterns of PACT-PKR interaction as hyperosmotic treatment with sucrose.
source: We demonstrated above that DSS treatment of cells in culture results in similar patterns of PACT-PKR interaction as hyperosmotic treatment with sucrose (Figure 1C), and that the PKR-mediated signaling promotes the inflammatory phenotype in DSS-treated mice (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1C shows PACT-PKR interaction with both DSS and sucrose treatments.

claim: PKR-mediated signaling promotes the inflammatory phenotype in DSS-treated mice.
source: We demonstrated above that DSS treatment of cells in culture results in similar patterns of PACT-PKR interaction as hyperosmotic treatment with sucrose (Figure 1C), and that the PKR-mediated signaling promotes the inflammatory phenotype in DSS-treated mice (Farabaugh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: Wild type MEFs showed Slc38a2 induction after a low intensity of DSS treatment, while NF-κB c-Rel-deficient MEFs lost this induction.
source: We found that while wild type MEFs showed Slc38a2 induction after a low intensity of DSS treatment, similar to the low-intensity sucrose treatment, while NF-κB c-Rel-deficient MEFs lost this induction of the adaptive Slc38a2 mRNA (Figure 3A).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 3A shows Slc38a2 induction in control cells but not in shc-Rel cells at 5% DSS.

claim: Loss of SNAT2 mRNA induction in shc-Rel MEFs led to a decrease of both the unprocessed immature and mature forms of SNAT2 protein.
source: This loss of SNAT2 mRNA induction in shc-Rel MEFs led to a decrease of both the unprocessed immature and mature forms of SNAT2 protein (Figure 3B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3B shows reduced SNAT2 protein in shc-Rel cells treated with DSS.

claim: DSS-treated shc-Rel MEFs show decreased GADD34 protein levels.
source: Also similar to sucrose-treated MEFs, DSS-treated shc-Rel MEFs show decreased GADD34 protein levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3C shows reduced GADD34 protein in shc-Rel cells treated with DSS.

claim: RAW macrophages treated with DSS display induction of osmoadaptive genes SNAT2 and GADD34 at low intensity treatment.
source: RAW macrophages treated with DSS display induction of osmoadaptive genes SNAT2 and GADD34 at low intensity treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 3D shows induction of Slc38a2 and Ppp1r15a in RAW macrophages at 5% DSS.

claim: Primary tracheal epithelial cells displayed induction of osmoadaptive genes in response to low-intensity treatment with NaCl.
source: Primary tracheal epithelial cells also displayed this pattern of gene expression in response to low-intensity treatment with NaCl (Figure 3E), indicating that this gene expression program appears to be universal.
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 3E shows induction of Slc38a2 and Ppp1r15a in tracheal epithelial cells at 400 mOsm NaCl.

claim: The osmoadaptive gene expression program appears to be universal across cell types and osmolytes.
source: Primary tracheal epithelial cells also displayed this pattern of gene expression in response to low-intensity treatment with NaCl (Figure 3E), indicating that this gene expression program appears to be universal.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from observing similar gene expression patterns in different cell types and with different osmolytes.

claim: 10,443 unique mRNAs were sequenced in the RNA-seq experiment.
source: 10,443 unique mRNAs were sequenced, and their expression profiles were visualized in a heatmap (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 3963 total genes were differentially expressed (p<0.05) between low-intensity and high-intensity treatment.
source: While 3963 total genes were differentially expressed (p<0.05) between low-intensity and high-intensity treatment, 2733 of these genes were also differentially expressed between iso-osmolar and hyperosmolar samples of both low and high intensity (Figure 4B), indicating a subset of genes differentially expressed in stress conditions independent of stress intensity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 2733 genes were differentially expressed between iso-osmolar and hyperosmolar samples of both low and high intensity, indicating a subset of genes differentially expressed in stress conditions independent of stress intensity.
source: While 3963 total genes were differentially expressed (p<0.05) between low-intensity and high-intensity treatment, 2733 of these genes were also differentially expressed between iso-osmolar and hyperosmolar samples of both low and high intensity (Figure 4B), indicating a subset of genes differentially expressed in stress conditions independent of stress intensity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The most significant common pathways among genes induced at high-intensity but not at low-intensity hyperosmotic stress were associated with changes in the ribosome (n = 75, p=8.40×10−51) and oxidative phosphorylation (n = 31, p=2.20×10−9).
source: The most significant common pathways among genes induced at high-intensity but not at low-intensity hyperosmotic stress were associated with changes in the ribosome (n = 75, p=8.40×10−51) and oxidative phosphorylation (n = 31, p=2.20×10−9)(Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis results are stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The most significant increase (p=6.68×10−257) of a gene after high intensity treatment that was not increased at low intensity treatment occurred in Hexim1.
source: The most significant increase (p=6.68×10−257) of a gene after high intensity treatment that was not increased at low intensity treatment occurred in Hexim1 (Figure 4C), a transcriptional elongation factor that has been shown to suppress tumor growth in response to nucleotide stresses (Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hexim1 is a transcriptional elongation factor that has been shown to suppress tumor growth in response to nucleotide stresses.
source: The most significant increase (p=6.68×10−257) of a gene after high intensity treatment that was not increased at low intensity treatment occurred in Hexim1 (Figure 4C), a transcriptional elongation factor that has been shown to suppress tumor growth in response to nucleotide stresses (Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2016.

claim: The most significantly increased genes at low intensity versus high intensity include GADD34 (Ppp1r15a) (p=2.77×10−250) and SNAT2 (Slc38a2) (p=6.45×10−290).
source: However, the most significantly increased genes at low intensity versus high intensity have more direct relevance to the aforementioned novel osmoadaptive response, including GADD34 (Ppp1r15a) (p=2.77×10−250) and SNAT2 (Slc38a2) (p=6.45×10−290), as well as NF-κB pathway negative feedback inhibitors IκBα (Nfkbia) (p=7.34×10−300) and A20 (Tnfaip3) (p=6.97×10−167) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The most significantly increased genes at low intensity versus high intensity include NF-κB pathway negative feedback inhibitors IκBα (Nfkbia) (p=7.34×10−300) and A20 (Tnfaip3) (p=6.97×10−167).
source: However, the most significantly increased genes at low intensity versus high intensity have more direct relevance to the aforementioned novel osmoadaptive response, including GADD34 (Ppp1r15a) (p=2.77×10−250) and SNAT2 (Slc38a2) (p=6.45×10−290), as well as NF-κB pathway negative feedback inhibitors IκBα (Nfkbia) (p=7.34×10−300) and A20 (Tnfaip3) (p=6.97×10−167) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Some TonEBP targets, including Hspa1a and Mmp9, displayed dependence on both TonEBP and NF-κB c-Rel.
source: Some TonEBP targets, including Hspa1a and Mmp9, displayed dependence on both TonEBP and NF-κB c-Rel (Figure 5B), hinting at the existence of a subset of genes that are targets of a TonEBP/NF-κB c-Rel complex.
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5B shows reduced Hspa1a and Mmp9 mRNA in both TonEBP KO and shc-Rel cells.

claim: Other osmoadaptive TonEBP targets, such as aldose reductase (Akr1b1) and the taurine transporter (Slc6a6) were not influenced by NF-κB c-Rel.
source: Other osmoadaptive TonEBP targets, such as aldose reductase (Akr1b1) and the taurine transporter (Slc6a6) were not influenced by NF-κB c-Rel (Figure 5C), indicating the regulation of a subset of these adaptive genes is NF-κB c-Rel-independent and likely are targets of TonEBP homodimers (Stroud et al., 2002).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5C shows similar Akr1b1 and Slc6a6 mRNA levels in shc-Rel and control cells.

claim: A subset of adaptive genes are NF-κB c-Rel-independent and likely are targets of TonEBP homodimers.
source: Other osmoadaptive TonEBP targets, such as aldose reductase (Akr1b1) and the taurine transporter (Slc6a6) were not influenced by NF-κB c-Rel (Figure 5C), indicating the regulation of a subset of these adaptive genes is NF-κB c-Rel-independent and likely are targets of TonEBP homodimers (Stroud et al., 2002).
evidence: This inference is drawn from the observation that some TonEBP targets are not affected by c-Rel depletion, and is supported by citation to Stroud et al., 2002.

claim: A third subset of genes displayed dependence on TonEBP and NF-κB p65 at high-intensity stress, including Elf3, Irf1, and Tnfrsf9.
source: A third subset of genes displayed dependence on TonEBP and NF-κB p65 at high-intensity stress, including Elf3, Irf1, and Tnfrsf9 (Figure 5D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5D shows reduced Elf3, Irf1, and Tnfrsf9 mRNA in both TonEBP KO and p65 KO cells at 600 mOsm.

claim: Il6 mRNA levels are dependent on NF-κB p65 in hyperosmotic stress conditions.
source: We have previously shown that Il6 mRNA levels are dependent on NF-κB p65 in hyperosmotic stress conditions (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and here also show that it is dependent on TonEBP (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Farabaugh et al., 2017).

claim: Il6 mRNA levels are dependent on TonEBP in hyperosmotic stress conditions.
source: We have previously shown that Il6 mRNA levels are dependent on NF-κB p65 in hyperosmotic stress conditions (Farabaugh et al., 2017), and here also show that it is dependent on TonEBP (Figure 5D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5D shows reduced Il6 mRNA in TonEBP KO cells.

claim: Some genes (Slc38a2, Mmp9, Hspa1a, Pppar15a) were positive targets of NF-κB c-Rel/TonEBP, and others (Il6, Elf3, Irf1, Tnfrsf9) were positive targets of NF-κB p65/TonEBP.
source: We concluded that some genes (Slc38a2, Mmp9, Hspa1a, Pppar15a) were positive targets of NF-κB c-Rel/TonEBP, and others (Il6, Elf3, Irf1, Tnfrsf9) were positive targets of NF-κB p65/TonEBP (Figure 5E).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the gene expression data showing differential dependence on c-Rel vs p65.

claim: There is competition between NF-κB p65 and NF-κB c-Rel for TonEBP interaction.
source: These data suggest that there is competition between NF-κB p65 and NF-κB c-Rel for TonEBP interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different genes are targets of different TonEBP complexes.

claim: NF-κB p65/TonEBP target genes that showed reduced induction upon loss of PACT include Il6, Elf3, Irf1, and Tnfrsf9.
source: These NF-κB p65/TonEBP targets that showed reduced induction upon loss of PACT include Il6 (Figure 1E), Elf3, Irf1, and Tnfrsf9 (Figure 5F).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 1E and Figure 5F shows reduced mRNA levels of these genes in shPACT cells.

claim: Several additional proinflammatory genes, including Ccl2, Cxcl1, and Icam-1, were discovered to have a dependence on PACT-mediated signaling.
source: Several additional proinflammatory genes, including Ccl2, Cxcl1, and Icam-1, were also discovered to have a dependence on PACT-mediated signaling, as evidenced by loss of their induction in PACT-deficient cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A shows reduced mRNA levels of these genes in shPACT cells.

claim: TonEBP/NF-κB p65 interaction promotes expression of proinflammatory targets of NF-κB p65, but not expression of osmoadaptive targets of TonEBP in response to TNF or LPS treatment.
source: It has been previously shown that TonEBP/NF-κB p65 interaction promotes expression of proinflammatory targets of NF-κB p65, but not expression of osmoadaptive targets of TonEBP in response to TNF or LPS treatment (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2017.

claim: An increase in stress intensity increases the levels of NF-κB p65/TonEBP complexes.
source: We observed that an increase in stress intensity increases the levels of NF-κB p65/TonEBP complexes (Figure 6B, right).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows increased TonEBP binding to p65 at 600 mOsm.

claim: There was an inverse correlation to complexes of NF-κB p65/NF-κB c-Rel, which were observed at iso-osmolar and low intensity-hyperosmotic conditions and lost upon high intensity-hyperosmotic treatment.
source: Interestingly, there was an inverse correlation to complexes of NF-κB p65/NF-κB c-Rel, which were observed at iso-osmolar and low intensity-hyperosmotic conditions and lost upon high intensity-hyperosmotic treatment.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows c-Rel binding to p65 at low intensity but not at high intensity.

claim: Activation of the PACT/PKR signaling axis promotes the loss of interaction of TonEBP with NF-κB c-Rel and the gain of interaction of TonEBP with NF-κB p65.
source: We also found that activation of the PACT/PKR signaling axis promotes the loss of interaction of TonEBP with NF-κB c-Rel and the gain of interaction of TonEBP with NF-κB p65, as shPACT MEFs retain some NF-κB p65/NF-κB c-Rel complexes and NF-κB p65/TonEBP complex formation is diminished (Figure 6B).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B shows altered complex formation in shPACT cells.

claim: TonEBP/NF-κB p65 interaction still occurs in shPACT MEFs at high stress intensity, suggesting that PACT signaling determines the amplitude of the response, not merely whether the response occurs.
source: We observed that TonEBP/NF-κB p65 interaction still occurs in shPACT MEFs at high stress intensity; this suggests that PACT signaling determines the amplitude of the response, not merely whether the response occurs.
evidence: This inference is drawn from the observation that TonEBP/p65 complexes are still present but reduced in shPACT cells.

claim: MEFs transfected with FLAG-c-Rel accumulated complexes of NF-κB c-Rel/NF-κB p65 and NF-κB c-Rel/TonEBP at iso-osmolar and low-intensity hyperosmotic conditions, and lose these complexes at high-intensity stress.
source: This finding was corroborated by the inverse experiment, in which MEFs transfected with FLAG-c-Rel were also found to accumulate complexes of NF-κB c-Rel/NF-κB p65 and NF-κB c-Rel/TonEBP at iso-osmolar and low-intensity hyperosmotic conditions, and lose these complexes at high-intensity stress (Figure 6C).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6C shows c-Rel complexes at low intensity but not at high intensity.

claim: PKRi treatment promoted the maintenance of NF-κB c-Rel/TonEBP and NF-κB c-Rel/NF-κB p65 complexes even at high intensity hyperosmotic stress.
source: While FLAG-tagged NF-κB c-Rel did not pull down TonEBP or NF-κB p65 in high-intensity hyperosmotic conditions in untreated cells, PKRi treatment promoted the maintenance of these complexes even at high intensity hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6D).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6D shows c-Rel complexes maintained at high intensity with PKRi treatment.

claim: Reconstitution of PACT KO MEFs with PACT bearing phosphosite mutations S246A or S287A shifted the makeup of Rel-homology domain complexes to resemble the composition in a low stress intensity.
source: In addition, reconstitution of PACT KO MEFs with PACT bearing phosphosite mutations S246A or S287A demonstrated that loss of PACT functionality in PKR activation also shifted the makeup of Rel-homology domain complexes to resemble the composition in a low stress intensity (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6E-F shows altered complex formation with PACT mutants.

claim: Activation of the PACT/PKR axis promotes dissociation of NF-κB p65 and TonEBP from NF-κB c-Rel in a manner dependent on stress intensity.
source: Together, these data indicate that activation of the PACT/PKR axis promotes dissociation of NF-κB p65 and TonEBP from NF-κB c-Rel in a manner dependent on stress intensity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing stress intensity-dependent complex formation.

claim: Levels of nuclear NF-κB p65 and NF-κB c-Rel both increased upon hyperosmotic treatment, particularly at high intensity treatment.
source: We found that levels of nuclear NF-κB p65 and NF-κB c-Rel both increased upon hyperosmotic treatment, particularly at high intensity treatment (Figure 7A, left).
evidence: Western blot data of nuclear fractions in Figure 7A shows increased p65 and c-Rel at high intensity.

claim: Upon loss of NF-κB c-Rel, the percentage of nuclear NF-κB p65 over total cellular NF-κB was basally higher (12%) than in control cells (1%) prior to low-intensity stress, and increased to a much higher percentage (43%) than in control cells (19%).
source: Upon loss of NF-κB c-Rel, the percentage of nuclear NF-κB p65 over total cellular NF-κB was basally higher (12%) than in control cells (1%) prior to low-intensity stress, and increased to a much higher percentage (43%) than in control cells (19%) (Figure 7A, middle).
evidence: Quantification of western blot data in Figure 7A shows these percentages.

claim: Upon loss of PACT, accumulation of c-Rel in the nucleus were greater after low intensity-hyperosmotic treatment (29%) than in control cells (8%).
source: Upon loss of PACT, accumulation of c-Rel in the nucleus were greater after low intensity-hyperosmotic treatment (29%) than in control cells (8%) (Figure 7A, right).
evidence: Quantification of western blot data in Figure 7A shows these percentages.

claim: After high intensity hyperosmotic treatments, 86% of total cellular NF-κB c-Rel and over 75% of total NF-κB p65 are found in the cytoplasm.
source: It is important to note that after high intensity hyperosmotic treatments, 86% of total cellular NF-κB c-Rel and over 75% of total NF-κB p65 are found in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is calculated from the quantification data in Figure 7A.

claim: NF-κB p65 and c-Rel species may not be the major transcription factors activated to translocate to the nucleus in response to hyperosmotic stress.
source: This suggests that NF-κB p65 and c-Rel species may not be the major transcription factors activated to translocate to the nucleus in response to hyperosmotic stress (Figure 7A, left).
evidence: This inference is drawn from the observation that most NF-κB remains in the cytoplasm.

claim: The interaction between NF-κB c-Rel and TonEBP is detected in the nucleus in basal conditions and in response to low-intensity hyperosmotic stress.
source: Despite the majority of NF-κB proteins remaining in the cytoplasm (Figure 7A), the interaction between NF-κB c-Rel and TonEBP is still detected in the nucleus in basal conditions and in response to low-intensity hyperosmotic stress (Figure 7B, left).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data from nuclear fractions in Figure 7B shows c-Rel/TonEBP complexes at low intensity.

claim: The loss of PACT leads to maintenance of NF-κB c-Rel/TonEBP complexes in the nucleus in response to high-intensity hyperosmotic stress.
source: The loss of PACT leads to maintenance of these complexes in response to high-intensity hyperosmotic stress (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data from nuclear fractions in Figure 7B shows c-Rel/TonEBP complexes maintained in shPACT cells at high intensity.

claim: In low intensity hyperosmotic conditions, TonEBP/NF-κB c-Rel complexes migrate to the nucleus and induce transcription of genes including SNAT2 and GADD34 that contribute to osmoadaptation and cell survival.
source: These data suggest that both PKR activation and NF-κB signaling are key components in the determination of cell fate in response to hyperosmotic stress. In low intensity hyperosmotic conditions, TonEBP/NF-κB c-Rel complexes migrate to the nucleus and induce transcription of genes including SNAT2 and GADD34 that contribute to osmoadaptation and cell survival.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: As intensity increases, PACT will bind to PKR, leading to its phosphorylation and subsequent activation.
source: As intensity increases, PACT will bind to PKR, leading to its phosphorylation and subsequent activation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: PACT-PKR activation correlates with a loss of TonEBP/NF-κB c-Rel and NF-κB p65/NF-κB c-Rel complexes, and instead an accumulation of TonEBP/NF-κB p65 complexes with potential to induce transcription of proinflammatory genes such as IL6 and Tnfrsf9.
source: This correlates with a loss of TonEBP/NF-κB c-Rel and NF-κB p65/NF-κB c-Rel complexes, and instead an accumulation of TonEBP/NF-κB p65 complexes with potential to induce transcription of proinflammatory genes such as IL6 and Tnfrsf9 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7C.

claim: PACT-PKR interaction is necessary for PKR activation and the expression of inflammatory genes and cell death under hyperosmotic conditions.
source: In this study, we have shown that PACT-PKR interaction is necessary for PKR activation and the expression of inflammatory genes and cell death under hyperosmotic conditions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: PACT-PKR signaling promotes proinflammatory gene expression in a stress intensity-dependent manner, via the modulation of interactions among members of the Rel-homology-domain family of transcription factors.
source: Our findings suggest a mechanism in which PACT-PKR signaling promotes proinflammatory gene expression in a stress intensity-dependent manner, via the modulation of interactions among members of the Rel-homology-domain family of transcription factors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: In low intensity hyperosmotic stress, NF-κB subunit c-Rel forms complexes with Rel-homology domain transcription factor TonEBP.
source: Specifically, we show that in low intensity hyperosmotic stress, NF-κB subunit c-Rel forms complexes with Rel-homology domain transcription factor TonEBP.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: NF-κB c-Rel/TonEBP interaction preserves adaptive signaling at low-intensity stress via the induced transcription of SNAT2 and its positive regulator, GADD34.
source: This interaction preserves adaptive signaling at low-intensity stress via the induced transcription of a key factor in the adaptive response, SNAT2, and its positive regulator, GADD34.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The loss of NF-κB c-Rel/TonEBP complexes at high-intensity stress may lead to increased TonEBP interaction with NF-κB p65 and subsequent increased expression of proinflammatory genes such as IL6 and Tnfrsf9.
source: The loss of these complexes at high-intensity stress may lead to increased TonEBP interaction with NF-κB p65 and subsequent increased expression of proinflammatory genes such as IL6 and Tnfrsf9.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The conservation of loss of adaptive (Slc38a2, Ppp1r15a) gene expression indicates conserved expression programs in response to hyperosmotic stress.
source: The conservation of this loss of adaptive (Slc38a2, Ppp1r15a) gene expression indicates conserved expression programs in response to hyperosmotic stress.
